strengths: Introduces and clearly formalizes a novel failure mode, 'contextual contradiction', distinguishing it from direct semantic contradiction, and supports the definition with an insightful attention-map analysis (Fig. 3) showing how entangled concepts compete for spatial attention.

The proposed Stage-Aware Prompting (SAP) method is training-free, architecture-agnostic, and simple to integrate at inference time, demonstrated to work on both FLUX and SD3 backbones with consistent gains.

Strong empirical validation: quantitative VLM-based alignment scores across three benchmarks, a substantial user study (61 participants, 1464 pairwise judgments) showing high win rates over multiple baselines in both alignment and visual quality, and informative ablations isolating the contribution of in-context examples, explanation requirement, and number of proxies.

Provides two new/curated benchmarks (Whoops-Hard and ContraBench) targeted specifically at contextual contradictions, which could be useful to the community for future evaluation of compositional/semantic alignment.

Includes a thoughtful robustness analysis (perturbing LLM-predicted timestep boundaries) and a failure-mode breakdown (Table 7) that transparently attributes most residual errors to LLM proxy-assignment mistakes vs. underlying model limitations, adding credibility to the analysis.
Clear qualitative illustrations (Figs. 4, 6, 7) intuitively explain why stage-aware conditioning helps, tying the method back to the coarse-to-fine denoising hypothesis.
weaknesses: The evaluation partially relies on GPT-4o for both generating the method's proxy prompts and scoring output alignment (as the primary quantitative metric), raising a potential circularity/self-consistency bias concern; the paper would benefit from an additional non-LLM alignment metric (e.g., CLIPScore/text-image similarity) to corroborate GPT-4o-based scores.

ContraBench is small (40 prompts) and was constructed using ChatGPT-generated candidates filtered by human annotators, which may bias the benchmark toward cases the LLM-based decomposition method is naturally suited to resolve.

The stage-to-timestep mapping used in the LLM instruction (Table 8) is a fairly coarse, manually specified heuristic (fixed step ranges assuming T=50); while shown robust to small perturbations, its generalization to substantially different sampler schedules, step counts, or model families beyond FLUX/SD3 is not deeply examined.

Ablation results show that a majority (63.3%) of residual failures stem from incorrect LLM proxy assignment, indicating the method's performance ceiling is tightly coupled to LLM reasoning quality; this dependency and its implications for reliability/reproducibility with weaker LLMs deserves more discussion (only briefly touched on via the LLaMA comparison in the appendix).

Baseline comparisons, while reasonable, are limited to a handful of prompt-conditioning/guidance methods (Ella, Annealing, R2F, VL-DNP) and do not include more recent region- or layout-based compositional control approaches, limiting the breadth of the comparison.

The paper does not analyze potential added inference latency/complexity beyond a brief note on the one-time LLM call, and does not discuss edge cases where mid-generation prompt switching could introduce visible discontinuities or artifacts at switch boundaries beyond isolated qualitative examples.
